items.title: Introducing Wolfram AI Course Assistant
items.summary:
Meet Wolfram AI Course Assistant—your lesson-aware AI study companion. It can explain course concepts, answer questions about the specific lesson you have open, and even write and run Wolfram Language code. See how it helps clarify topics like Riemann sums and integrals, modify lesson code, and suggest lesson-specific prompts to deepen learning. Available with all tiers of Wolfram AI Access, including the free Basic plan with any active license.

items.title: How to Remember AI Concepts for the Long Term
items.summary:
Learning AI concepts is one thing. Remembering them weeks or months later is another.

In this short, Luis Serrano, author of Grokking Machine Learning, Second Edition, shares a simple way to make machine learning ideas stick — by building intuition, connecting concepts visually, and practicing them in ways your brain can actually remember.

If you want AI and ML to feel less like memorization and more like understanding, this one’s for you.

Book: https://hubs.la/Q04rsqf30

items.title: Why did fine-tuning never really take off with OpenAI's API?
items.summary:
Why did fine-tuning never really take off with OpenAI's API?

Lin Qiao, CEO of Fireworks, says the reason is not technical but economical. Training a frontier model costs so much that the only way the math works is selling one model to everyone. Supporting millions of custom fine-tuned versions is a completely different business, and it's just not what the big labs are built to do.

items.title: Predictive AI and GenAI, Side by Side | H2O.ai Managed Cloud
items.summary:
Fraud detection, demand forecasting, document intelligence, and retrieval-augmented generation all run on the same platform, under the same governance model.

This lesson maps what you can actually build on H2O.ai Managed Cloud. The platform is structured around three pillars: modelling and automation, where models get built and refined; AI applications and data engineering, where models become systems people can use; and deployment, monitoring, and governance, where AI runs reliably in production.

Within that structure, predictive AI answers what is likely to happen, and generative AI answers how you can generate, reason, and automate knowledge. Both work across structured data like transactions and time series, and unstructured data like text, images, and audio.

Covered in this video:
The three platform pillars and what each one is responsible for
Predictive AI use cases: fraud detection, demand forecasting, credit risk, churn prediction, anomaly detection
Generative AI use cases: enterprise assistants, document intelligence, summarization, RAG, agentic workflows
How operationalization is built in, covering secure deployment, scalable infrastructure, monitoring, and governance

LINKS

Documentation: https://docs.h2o.ai

H2O.ai builds the platform enterprises use to develop, deploy, and operate AI on their own private data, across predictive machine learning and generative AI.

items.title: Employee Facing AI Paid Off First
items.summary: In episode 1017 of the SuperDataScience Podcast, Jon Krohn talks with Pete Johnson, Field CTO at MongoDB, about why four out of five organizations with AI steering committees still see no return on their AI investment. Pete reveals that successful AI deployments focus on employee-facing, human-in-the-loop use cases, where existing performance metrics allow for direct attribution of AI's impact, making it easier to measure and prove ROI.

items.title: Anyone Can Make Amazing Games Now (Easy)
items.summary:
I vibe coded a full game sequel using Claude Code and Codex, and it proved something important about AI and game development.

A year ago I built The Librarian, a playable vibe coded game you can still find on GitHub. This time I wanted to see how far AI coding tools have come, and whether one person could build something that actually feels like a real game.

I used Claude Code with Opus 5 for the initial build, then switched to Codex and GPT-5.6 Sol for all the fine-tuning. The result is The Librarian 2, a 3D procedurally generated roguelite with boss enemies, natural disasters, meta progression, and a chaos system. 10,400 lines of code across 33 modules. Zero asset files.

The verdict: game development is far from cooked. But it's also a lot harder than the one-level demos on X make it look.
